newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian communist chief criticises summit results.
newsitem.headline: Russian communist chief criticises summit results.

text.p: Russian Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said on Friday the summit meeting between President Boris Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki had dealt Moscow a "crushing defeat", Interfax news agency said.

Zyuganov, Yeltsin's strongest rival in last year's presidential election, compared the results of the meeting with the humiliating Versailles Treaty of 1919 which ended World War One and set humiliating conditions for Germany, the loser.
"Yeltsin's foreign policy suffered a crushing defeat," Interfax quoted Zyuganov as saying. "In fact the Helsinki agreements are Russia's Versailles."

Yeltsin and Clinton agreed in Helsinki on Friday to differ on the eastward expansion of NATO, but said Moscow would still negotiate a partnership agreement with the alliance which they hoped all allied leaders would sign before a July NATO summit.

Yeltsin reaffirmed Moscow's view that admitting ex-communist Warsaw Pact states to NATO would be "a serious mistake", but he chose instead to stress progress on arms control, NATO-Russia relations and Moscow's integration into international economic institutions.
"The (partnership) agreement with NATO will change little for Russia," Zyuganov said.

"The real fact is that Russia was admitted to NATO's anteroom but it is not taken seriously any longer," he added, referring to the western alliance's intention to go ahead with the enlargement despite Moscow's objections.
Yeltsin and his conservative foes were equally critical of NATO's plans to grant membership to Moscow's Cold War allies.

But in contrast to Yeltsin, who focused on working out a deal to ensure at least some of Moscow's interests were met after it had failed to stop the expansion, Russian hardliners have insisted on uncompromising opposition whatever the result.

"The real deal would be a situation when none of the countries liberated by the Soviet Union from Nazis in the World War Two could join any military block for another 200 years," Ekho Moskvy news agency quoted Zyuganov as saing in a separate interview.
